## .length vs .size() vs .length()

| | Type | Used on | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.length` | Field | Arrays only | `arr.length` |
| `.length()` | Method | String only | `"hello".length()` |
| `.size()` | Method | Collections only | `list.size()`, `map.size()`, `set.size()` |

Memory hook: arrays/Strings → `.length` / `.length()`. Collections (List, Map, Set) → always `.size()`.

## PriorityQueue & Comparators

| Comparator | Heap type | Top element |
|---|---|---|
| `new PriorityQueue<>()` | Min-heap (default) | Smallest |
| `(a, b) -> a - b` | Min-heap | Smallest |
| `(a, b) -> b - a` | Max-heap | Largest |
| `Collections.reverseOrder()` | Max-heap | Largest |

**How to read a comparator:** negative return → first argument has priority.
- `a - b` negative when `a < b` → smaller values win → min-heap
- `b - a` negative when `b < a` → larger values win → max-heap

**The comparator IS what defines min/max.** There's no separate flag — you don't combine a heap type with a comparator.

**Custom comparator on object field:**
```java
PriorityQueue<Product> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.price - b.price); // min-heap by price
```

**Top K pattern rule:**
- Top K largest → min-heap of size K (peek = cheapest of top K = eviction candidate)
- Top K smallest → max-heap of size K (peek = largest of top K = eviction candidate)

Counter-intuitive: heap type matches what you want to *evict*, not what you want to *keep*.

```java
// Keep top 3 most expensive products
PriorityQueue<Product> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.price - b.price); // min-heap
if (pq.size() < 3) pq.offer(product);
else if (product.price > pq.peek().price) { pq.poll(); pq.offer(product); }
```
